title: Refs (useRef)
definition: The `useRef` hook returns a mutable ref object whose `.current` property is initialized to the passed argument. It is used to persist values across renders without causing a re-render, or to directly access DOM elements.
simpleExplanation: Imagine you have a sticky note on your desk. `useState` is like writing a number on the main whiteboard (everyone sees it, and writing on it stops the whole class). `useRef` is like writing a number on your private sticky note. You can change it secretly as much as you want, and the teacher (React) will never stop the class (re-render) because of it.
realWorldExample: You want a text input to automatically be focused (cursor blinking) when a modal opens. You use `useRef` to grab the actual HTML `<input>` element and call `inputRef.current.focus()`.
useCases: Directly accessing and manipulating DOM elements (focus, measuring size)
Storing mutable values that shouldn't trigger re-renders (like a timer ID)
Keeping track of previous state values

basic: What is the primary difference between `useState` and `useRef`?

intermediate: If you update `myRef.current = 5`, will the component re-render?

answers.question: What is the primary difference between useState and useRef?
answers.answer: Changing state triggers a component re-render. Changing a ref's `.current` value does NOT trigger a re-render. State is for data that affects the UI; Refs are for background data or DOM nodes.

answers.question: When is the .current property attached to the DOM element?
answers.answer: React assigns the DOM element to `.current` after the component has rendered, but before `useEffect` fires. So it is perfectly safe to access it inside `useEffect`.

answers.question: Is useRef the same as just creating an object { current: value }?
answers.answer: No. If you create a regular object, a brand new object is created on every render. `useRef` guarantees that you will get the exact same object reference across every single render.
